name: Vector Graphics and Interface Assets
title: Vector Graphics and Interface Assets
answer: Vector graphics and interface assets cover anything drawn as paths, curves, strokes and fills rather than pixels: icons, logos, pictograms, diagrams, maps, type, and the illustration and component art that sits inside a product interface. The work spans a family of outputs, from a single SVG glyph to a full icon set, an empty-state illustration, or a design system's worth of shapes that must stay consistent at many sizes. It sits in the visual arts because composition, weight and legibility still matter, and in engineering because the same file often ships as code. Practitioners here are usually designers who think in grids and layers, not machine learning engineers.

Practitioners here are usually designers who think in grids and layers, not machine learning engineers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The toolchain is a mix of editors and code. Figma, Adobe Illustrator, Inkscape and Affinity Designer are the common drawing environments, and SVG is the format most of this work travels in, rendered by browsers and rasterized by GPUs at display time. On the generative side, most current systems produce a raster image first and then trace it into paths, while a smaller set of models emit path commands or markup directly. Because vector files are text, they diff, merge and version well, which makes them a natural fit for repositories, build pipelines and component libraries. Optimization passes such as SVGO and sprite or symbol assembly are routine steps before anything ships.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical generative workflow starts with a prompt, a sketch or an existing reference, produces a raster candidate, then converts it to paths with a tracing step and cleans the result by hand or with simplification tools. The cleanup is where most of the craft lives: reducing node count, aligning to a pixel grid, normalizing stroke widths, unifying corner radii, and checking that the shape still reads at small sizes. Other routes skip tracing entirely, using language models that write SVG markup, parametric systems driven by templates and variables, or symbol libraries where a generator only chooses and arranges prebuilt parts. Whatever the route, the deliverable is usually reviewed in an editor, named and layered for the people who will maintain it, and exported in the formats the product needs.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions cluster around training data, style and marks. A model trained on scraped icon sets, fonts or illustration portfolios can reproduce distinctive shapes, and the line between influence and copying is part of what the broader wave of intellectual property litigation around generative models is testing, a wave this site currently tracks at 92 active suits. Trademark and logo similarity is a separate risk from copyright, and font licensing, open source licences and attribution requirements all attach to assets that look trivial to copy. Provenance practice is still thin: keeping records of prompts, source references, model versions and human edits helps a team answer questions later. Accessibility also belongs here, since contrast, labelling and scalable hit targets are part of whether an asset is usable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward vector output that arrives already structured, with named layers, editable paths and tokens that match a design system rather than a flat traced blob. Models that emit markup directly are improving, and the interesting work is less about drawing a single icon than about generating a coherent family that stays consistent across sizes, states and themes. Closer coupling between design tools and code seems likely, so that an asset and its component definition are produced and versioned together. Evaluation is the open problem, because judging a vector asset means judging editability and system fit, not just how the picture looks. With 1000 live image generation models tracked on this site, the bottleneck is shifting from generation to selection, review and maintenance.
